content.text: Introductory slide text includes UPS/FORTNA OptiSweep Training, Day 1, and date/time 2026-03-17 13:16 UTC.
Opening slide includes presenter names Mitchel Flynn and Samuel Prescott.
Related artifact is tagged as training, title-slide, presenters, and intro; visible text is session-identification content.
The segment transitions from informal conversation to: "All right, we'll get started. My name is Mitchell Flynn. This is Akron. We'll be going through this morning's slides."
Transcript includes discussion about people arriving, hearing each other, Wi-Fi availability, and room temperature before the session starts.
Artifact summary states the segment appears to capture pre-training attendee conversation and room logistics before the formal presentation begins.
Presenter says the session will go through just the overview and asks, 'So what is Opti Suite?' Slide OCR reads 'Overview What is Optisweep?'
Transcript says Chrome will go through Geek Plus and Jose, if he shows up, will do Aveva; otherwise the presenter will do it.
Presenter says the morning will cover 'just the overview' and references attendees who may not know the system.
FORTNA developed an automated Consolidated Bagging (ACB) solution utilizing AGVs and tippers to create a flexible and scalable bagging system.

In a traditional small sort system, operators are assigned sections of destinations (20-25) on a sorter; when a bag is full the operator closes the destination, prints and applies a label, zips the bag, places it on a takeaway belt, and reopens the chute.
In a Belted ACB solution when a destination is full the bin is dropped on a takeaway conveyor that conveys the packages as a slug down a chute into a bag station.

FORTNA wanted a more modular and adaptive design that would need little modification to existing sorters; by utilizing AGVs and tippers we can scale solutions and tailor maps to existing building sorters.
UPS has a standard communication through all buildings; all the sorters talk the same way and it goes onto a chat.
Our OptiSweep software integrates everything, so everything talks and works as a team.
Overview slide shows UPS Chat, tote tipper/tote tip stations, Geek+ AGVs, hospital controller, OptiSweep Software, sorter, printer, and Aveva HMI; transcript also mentions scan tunnel.
We have a hospital controller for you to remove and add totes.
UPS in all their buildings uses Aveva for HMIs.
Slide and transcript state that Geek+ AGVs operate over QR codes, are directly controlled by Geek+ RMS, and Geek+ handles all movement and route determination.
Transcript explains that inside the AGV are sensors and collision sensing, which report back to RMS, while RMS dictates what the robot needs to do and sends commands.
Transcript states that if the AGV sees an obstacle, the hardware reports it to RMS, and RMS generates an alarm code visible on the RMS screen.
Transcript says the office software, described as WCS, assigns robot tasks that go into a queue in RMS, and RMS executes them one by one by sending commands to the AGV.
Slide text states that the AGVs have forward collision sensors and that this version is intended to operate in a fenced system.
The segment introduces tote racks and explains that this is where the tote sits on the cylinder.
We have little feet so that when the tote drops, it is aligned to the center. It's pretty tight.
We also have these fins on the side that help move packages towards the center if they kind of hit.
OCR text references tote racking with a beveled design to securely position tote for parcel impact; transcript describes centering features.
Each station has two tippers; tipper will clamp tote from AGV, actuates tipping arm to dump contents onto chute, and places tote back onto AGV.
An HB will come in, the tipper will be clamped, actuators tip the arm to dump contents onto the chute; slide also states the tote is placed back onto AGV.
Self-contained HMI for operation and fault recovery.
Operators equipped with Estop and ready to tip buttons; transcript references a button that says 'I'm ready to tip.'
Operators equipped with Estop and ready to tip buttons.
Software slide lists OptiSweep software, AVEVA - HMI, Ignition - OPC Server, Chat XLE - UPS communications, and S-Tunnel - Encryption from OTNet to UPS Corp.
Ignition is described as the OPC server; OPC is confirmed as a protocol, and Ignition communicates through the tippers through OPC and feeds data to AVEVA.
Slide labels AVEVA as HMI, and the transcript says data is fed to AVEVA because it can directly integrate with the OPC server.
OptiSweep operates on OT net separate from the UPS network; WCS talks to UPS Chat XLE through S-Tunnel as a secure channel to get order and destination information.
Lifecycle of a sort: startup, bulk sort, bag-out, and shutdown with AGVs cycling to chargers.
AGVs start up in a shutdown state at specific charging locations; startup takes them from power cycling to staged for sort; shutdown cycles them back to the charger.
Bulk sort is where items are sorted and AGVs take full totes to tippers for bagging; bag-out cycles locations with remaining tote items to finish the sort.
The system will tell you with system faults; examples include an AGV waiting to do an exchange during shutdown or startup delay while waiting for an AGV on the charger.
Before parcels reach our system, they are unloaded from trailers in bulk onto a series of belts that lead to sorter induction.
This triggers the first message from Chat with a tracking ID, dimensions, and package type.
If this message fails and we see something unknown inducted, it is assigned default dimensions by OptiSweep.
This triggers the second message from Chat with a tracking Id, barcode data, dimensional data, and potential destination data.
Two thresholds exist: "Pretty full" — not full, but getting close enough to start considering an exchange; "Full" — no more product can be diverted to this location until an exchange is done.
When a tote is full, we tell Chat that the chute is unavailable so that no packages come down while doing an exchange.
OCR text references weight and dimensions, and says software determines how full a location or tote is as items sort; dimensions are scaled up by software based on package type.

Lifecycle of a parcel slide: parcels are unloaded onto belts leading to sorter induction; first Chat message contains tracking ID, dimensions, and package type; second message contains tracking ID, barcode data, dimensional data, and potential destination data.
Slide OCR: If this message fails and we see something unknown inducted, it is assigned default dimensions by OptiSweep.
Transcript: UPS gives this order multiple destinations; it is not a ZIP code, it is a sorted destination.
Slide OCR: second message includes potential destination data.
Transcript: a ZIP code can be mapped to a single destination or multiple destinations; this comes from the ASX system; the local system only knows where it needs to go.
A parcel will sort down to a chute location and into a tote; software adds that parcel to the tote located in that rack.

This triggers the next message from the chat... a divert confirm or sort confirmation. This message is pretty critical because if we don't get it, we don't actually know where it went or what's in the tote.
Software determines how full a tote is using weight and dimensions; dimensions are scaled by package type. Two thresholds exist: pretty full and full.
When a tote is full, we tell Chat that the chute is unavailable so that no packages come down while doing an exchange; at full threshold the chute is closed.
We don't have any photo eyes; there's no sensors at all, just weight and dimensions. If dimension data is missing, all the chutes can appear to overfill.
Off the end goes into a Gaylord at Hazleton; sort confirmations indicate two destinations off the end, allowing some tracking until the parcel is sorted or rejected and removed from tables.
The goal is to have one AGV come behind it and then move simultaneously together. One moves out, one moves in.
There's thresholds... Staging for an exchange can happen when a tote is immediately full or completely full, eminently filled.
An AGV with no tote that is designated to the tote zone moves under the racking to position for a lift. The tote is lifted in position.
This AGV that just dropped its tote will now become the AGV that will pick up the next tote.
We open the chute when the AGV moves in, not when it drops a tote... We have very strict quick KPI's we have to meet.

The front AGV will not move until AGV behind it; software sends both commands at the same time. If an AGV moves out without replacement, the AGV behind it likely faulted or was not backfilled properly.
The chute gets closed when the chute is full. Thresholds are staged so exchange occurs before 80%, with a goal of median 8 second exchange time and a floor of 6.7 seconds.
A full tote on an AGV is assigned a specific tipper using round robin to available enabled tippers serviced by the queue, then sent to the tipper entrance queue.
The AGV travels to the tip location and the software informs the tipper controller using OPC that the AGV has staged for a tip.

An operator pushes a button to start the tip. Software monitors tip progress and sends a chat message to prompt bag label printing. After the tip, the operator labels the bag, places it on a takeaway, and hangs the next empty bag.
When the full cycle is complete, the tipper informs the software that the AGV is clear to move; the AGV can return to the sorter, go to the hospital, or go to charge.
The tipper informs the software that the AGV is clear to move out when the full cycle is complete.
If there's an issue or it didn't clamp correctly, it goes to the hospital; slide text states 'Failed tip leads to Hospital.'
Low battery level leads to charger; the least charged AGVs are charged continuously to keep the system going through peak.
If all is good, the AGV returns to the sorter entrance queue with an empty tote that will be used for its next exchange.
If photo sensors do not see the tote correctly, or if the system cannot clamp down fully, it sends the item to the hospital.
The hospital is not a manned station; the supervisor bounces back and forth and nearby tipper positions may watch it.

The layout is designed for modularity and scalability, with distinct areas connected by a common entrance and exit. To move from one area to another, an AGV must go to the exit before entering the next.
OCR lists areas: Hospital, SorterSide, Charger, Tipper; narration says the layout has hospitals, sorter sides, chargers, and tippers.

Anything that wants to go into this area must go to the entrance queue first... queue locations... AGVs stage behind for an exchange... sorter queue locations... pick up the tote and leave into the aisle... after an exchange, it must go to the exit queue.

We have shutdown queues... these locations are under the rack... when you shut down, they move to shutdown locations... these locations are AGVs without totes... this location is for AGVs with totes... if you come into the entrance and we're in a shutdown state and you have a tote, you go to off the end and then you go to the shutdown.

Bag out works when you're done with the sort and need to bag out all locations... everything has to come out of the system... all chutes are closed... any tote with an item in it gets an exchange or marked for an exchange... in bag out it's just back to front... once completed, everything is out of the system and they're ready to start another sort.

You have sorts such as preload, day sort, and twilight... all these sorts have to be cycled in... they can't just run into each other because the volume is going to different locations... even in peak season, you still have those transitions.
The sorter side has zones... an AGV in a zone only picks up and drops off in its zone... comes into its zone, sees if anything needs to be exchanged, moves on... it's basically FIFO.
Transcript states tipper A and B are tip locations and each one has its own tipper queue; slide OCR shows modularization with tipper entrance and exit queues.
Transcript explains hospital entrance queue, drop-off if location is free, movement to pickup location, waiting if no tote is present, and then movement to exit queue.
Transcript says hospitals are used when an AGV cannot tip at the tipper, describes this as a reject state/detection, and says the hospital is used to initialize new AGVs and acts like a home base.
Transcript gives a shutdown-state example where removing an AGV without a tote and adding another AGV causes the new AGV to go through the hospital first and then determine where an AGV is missing.

Transcript says the charger has an entrance queue and tote locations where an AGV drops off its tote before charging, does not like to charge with totes on it, then picks up the tote and goes to the exit queue.
“the hospital is just a reject station for an operator to address those totes so that the packages get back”
“Shut down queues is just where it sits when it's shut down... when they start up, they move into their own zones”
The discussion references startup state, shutdown state, running state, and says “for the most part, you're either running, bagging out, or... close out originally.”
“once it's done with bag out, it will go to a running state” and “unless you choose to put the system shut down”
The speakers say shutdown is “something you choose from the HMI” and mention “using a Viva HMI” to put in a shutdown.
The segment says “we planned for peak” and discusses shutdown sending AGVs to charge, affecting how quickly the system can cycle again.
RMS is the robot management system... the brains behind the AGVs... The AGVs are just physical vehicles with some sensors on it, some encoders on it... So the RMS tells these AGVs what to do.
For each site, we're gonna have a Argus server and you're gonna access the RMS web location... it's the RMS web application and you're gonna have a unique IP address to access this RMS service.
Once you access that address, you put in the username and password... And this is what you will see. This is the overview screen.
Communication between RMS and what? And the OptiSweep it's API APIs. You mean REST API? Yes, REST API.
We've worked with Geek Plus for two years to use some custom APIs and also along with the existing APIs that they already have for tasks.

You can't bypass our software or else we get out of sync... if you have a problem and you want to bypass the OptiSweep service... the OptiSweep software doesn't know what happened. It has no knowledge of the database of that transaction.
Users will see buttons that help navigate around the RMS application, including language selection, a sidebar menu, and Map Monitor.
On the top right corner is your language selection; sometimes the default language is Chinese, and the third icon from the right can switch it to English.
The sidebar menu is sometimes hidden and can be expanded by clicking the referenced control; the slide also notes the menu can be expanded or collapsed.
The second option in the expanded menu is Map Monitor, where users will probably spend most of their time; the slide says Map Monitor allows viewing the map and AGV movements.
Clicking this view gives an overview of the system; the presenter references separating sorter side, charger side, and tipper side from this map.
The presenter says that in RMS world, a station is a station.
A special location could be a sort location and can also be a tipper location; the system does not know the difference by itself.
There are two variants of location: a lane, shown as light blue grayish square blocks, and stations, shown as orange ones.
Slide shows 'Map Monitor Message Panel' on the right side with robot counts, AGV fault items, disconnected AGV count, fault inspection, locate faulted AGV, and E-stop.
OCR lists 'Count of active Robots' and 'Count of Robots charging' in the Map Monitor message panel.
OCR lists AGV fault-related items: dropdown to show AGV faults, count of AGVs disconnected, inspection to view details of fault, and locate faulted AGV.
OCR includes 'E stop the system' as an item shown on the slide for the Map Monitor message panel.
Presenter says the right panel gives more information and the next slide will zoom into that right panel.
OCR weakly indicates a slide titled 'Map Overview' and the artifact retrieval text describes a map-style interface with a side panel.
Presenter says: 'that right panel ... will give you some more information.'
The first one is the open message panel... pending messages containing active errors or warnings... as well as the history of the alarms that it generated over maybe like the past 24-48 hours.

The second point, it's the active robot count... telling you how many robots you have that are actively running in the system... it says 10, which means that you have 10 robots in the system that are actively charging at the moment.

There's a small drop down here. Sometimes this is hidden, but if you have a current fault that needs to be addressed, it will show up here... you click that drop down menu and you will be able to see the errors.

The next one is the count of AGVs that are disconnected... AGVs have lost communication from RMS... RMS is the application running on the server... The AGVs are on the Wi-Fi... it can happen for multiple reasons... or it was turned off.

The shutdown state is different from turned off... shutdown is something... terminology that we use to define a state of the OptiSweep operation... I wouldn't call the AGV shut down. I'll call them turn off.

You can have AGVs in the system, but not in the map... if you turn off the AGV, that AGV will still appear on the map, but as a purple AGV, that means it's disconnected and it's still in the map... once you remove it, that AGV is no longer associated with the map that you're looking at, but it's still part of your system.
Additional icons help users understand paths and inspect map objects; the panel includes path, station ID, charger ID, and object selection icons.
View all AGV active paths shows all active paths on the map as a small blue line from the AGV to where it wants to go.
Stations are special locations with unique IDs; AGVs can go between stations using those IDs, and the IDs are important for debugging and identifying problems.
All chargers in the system have unique IDs, and clicking the charger ID icon displays them.
Certain map items are clickable, but users must first choose the object type to inspect from the left-side panel: robot, container, cell, or charger.
When a robot is selected, you can click on a robot and see details. If the detail section is hidden, a small arrow expands it. The selected robot has a box around it.

Important details include robot ID and location. The node code is pretty much the cell code for the robot. The panel can also show a tote ID, such as tote #96, as the unique identifier of the tote on the robot.

If the robot has a tote it will show under the robot ID. If the tote has a '?' before it, the robot has been removed but the tote has not. If a robot does not have a tote it will say layer_1, and the brown box is not shown.
Robot colors: Purple = robot disconnected; Blue/Flashing Blue = robot in task/searching for label; Green = robot not in a task; Red = fault/low battery.
Red means the robot has fault or a low battery, both of which will show up in the message panel.
Slide title appears as "Robot Selection Add and Remove" with sections for Add Robot and Remove Robot.
OCR text states: "Enter the corresponding robot ID" and for removal "Enter the corresponding robot Id or select the robot."
OCR text states the system will show that adding was successful and that removal was successful.
Slide shows 'Robot Selection' and 'Restart Robot' with text indicating entry of robot ID or selection of the robot, followed by clicking Restart.
Slide text states: 'The robot will restart (it is at the restart point or on the QR code cell).'
Slide text states that after starting, the positioned robot will be displayed on the station map.

If you want to add a certain robot on this tab over here, you type in the robot ID and you simply click the Add button... to remove a robot, you can either type in the robot ID or you can click on a robot itself and press remove.

If the robot is already in the system, nothing will happen, but once it's added successfully, the system will show that the robot was added successfully... if removal is successful, it will show the removal was successful.
You don't have a logical robot on the system, but you have a physical robot on the system.
Each robot has a right of way and space that it occupies on the map.
Any robot that is about to use that pathway think that space is empty and free, it will see that robot as an obstacle... It will not crash.
Slide shows Robot Selection with Add Robot and Remove Robot actions using robot ID entry and success confirmation.
Transcript notes typing the robot into the field below Robot and that partial ending digits can show matching robots if already introduced.
Any device connected on the OT network, whether a laptop or computer, will have access to the web software application through that IP.
Remote support will not have access to OT net unless authorized to use the UPS VPN through Z Scaler; after authorization, the site address or RMS address can be used to access Geek Plus RMS.
The shop floor has two HMI stations where this view is displayed for the local team, with one located at the hospital.

Transcript: 'you put in the ID or you select the robot that you're interested in restarting. You press the restart button on this panel over here'. OCR slide: 'Enter the corresponding robot Id or select the robot' and 'Click Restart'.

Transcript: 'if your robot is stopped for some reason in between two labels and you perform a restart, it will not snap back onto the map automatically... It's because it can't see a label.' Transcript references 'flashing blue sign', 'go from flashing blue to solid blue', and 'Once it's solid green... you have to wait till it turns green... because the brakes stay locked.'
Transcript: 'you have to wait till it turns green for you to move it because the brakes stay locked' and 'when it identifies a label... it will lock itself on the label'.

rough_steps: Open the RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui) and navigate to the AGV status/errors overview area. [Image support needed: screenshot of the RMS page showing the AGV status/errors overview table or panel.]

structured_payload.title: Verify Sorter Queue Routing: Entrance Queue → Queue Locations → Sorter Queue Locations → Exit Queue → Shutdown Queues
structured_payload.candidate_goal: Confirm that AGVs/totes follow the documented sorter queue routing sequence (entrance queue first, then exchange staging, then sorter queue pickup, then exit queue after exchange, and finally shutdown queue positioning based on tote presence).
structured_payload.summary: Turns the training description of sorter queue areas into an operator-support check: what each queue area is for and what the expected next queue should be after exchange and during shutdown entry (including the 'off the end' behavior when entering shutdown with a tote).
rough_steps: Identify the sorter queue areas in the live layout view used by support (entrance queue, queue locations for exchange staging, sorter queue locations for tote pickup/aisle entry, exit queue, shutdown queues). [Image support needed: the live screen/diagram that shows these named queue areas and their labels.]
Observe an AGV/tote that is entering the sorter area and confirm it first appears in the entrance queue (i.e., anything entering must go to the entrance queue first).
After the entrance queue, confirm the AGV/tote transitions to the queue locations area where AGVs stage behind for an exchange.
Confirm that after exchange staging, the tote is picked up at the sorter queue locations (described as where you pick up the tote and leave into the aisle).
After an exchange, confirm the AGV/tote goes to the exit queue (described as where it goes as it leaves before it could go to anywhere else for shutdown).

When the system is in shutdown, confirm shutdown queue positioning based on tote presence: AGVs without totes go to shutdown locations under the rack; AGVs with totes go to the shutdown location described as 'for AGVs with totes'.
If entering shutdown from the entrance while a tote is present, confirm the documented 'off the end' path occurs before the shutdown location (entrance → off the end → shutdown).
structured_payload.expected_result: For live activity, items follow the documented routing: entrance queue first, then exchange staging (queue locations), then sorter queue locations for tote pickup/aisle entry, then exit queue after exchange, and during shutdown the AGV/tote ends up in the correct shutdown location based on whether a tote is present (including the off-the-end step when entering shutdown with a tote).
failure_or_escalation_notes: Escalate if an AGV/tote appears to bypass the entrance queue, does not stage in the exchange queue locations before sorter pickup, does not go to the exit queue after exchange, or ends up in the wrong shutdown location for tote presence.
If the live layout view does not clearly label these queue areas, stop and use the site interview/visual confirmation to map the live labels to the documented queue names.

structured_payload.summary: The segment explains that the only time the front AGV can move without replacement is when the AGV behind it has a fault (software sends both commands together). Navigate to the Robot Selection screen that shows the Robot Selection Add and Remove controls. [Image support needed: screenshot/figure of the Robot Selection screen showing the Robot field, Add button, Remove section, and success message area.]
To add a robot: in the Robot ID entry field, enter the corresponding robot ID (the source indicates you can type the ID and that partial numeric entry may surface matching robots already introduced).

Click the "Add" button. [Image support needed: Robot Selection Add and Remove ! Robot x Robot « Add Robot = Cs . IBGGGE0RR0 , = 1. Enter the corresponding robot ID iBBRBRERESEE " 2. Click "Add" - to ae > a 3. The system will sh]
Verify the system displays an "adding was successful" confirmation message. [Image support needed: example of the success confirmation text/state after clicking Add.]
To remove a robot: enter the corresponding robot ID or select the robot from the list shown for that ID.

Click the "Remove" button. [Image support needed: Robot Selection Add and Remove ! Robot x Robot « Add Robot = Cs . IBGGGE0RR0 , = 1. Enter the corresponding robot ID iBBRBRERESEE " 2. Click "Add" - to ae > a 3. The system will sh]

failure_or_escalation_notes: If the success confirmation does not appear after clicking "Add" or "Remove", stop and escalate for support (the source does not provide troubleshooting steps for failures).
If you cannot access the Geek Plus RMS web application, verify OT network access or remote authorization via UPS VPN through Zscaler (the source only states access dependency, not remediation steps).

content.text: If a robot is restarted but does not snap back onto the map because it cannot see a label, use the documented indicator behavior (flashing blue → solid blue; solid green behavior) and perform the source-described physical label reacquisition steps, then clear the E stop and confirm the robot shows successfully on the map.

structured_payload.title: Handle restart when robot cannot see a label: use indicator color states and verify map visibility after label reacquisition
structured_payload.candidate_goal: Determine why a restarted robot is not snapping back onto the map (cannot see a label) and confirm recovery by observing the documented indicator color transitions and successful map display.
structured_payload.summary: If a robot is restarted but does not snap back onto the map because it cannot see a label, use the documented indicator behavior (flashing blue → solid blue; solid green behavior) and perform the source-described physical label reacquisition steps, then clear the E stop and confirm the robot shows successfully on the map.
rough_steps: After restarting, check whether the robot snaps back onto the map automatically. [Image support needed: map view showing the robot missing/not positioned after restart.]

If the robot is not on the map, look for the documented indicator state described as a “flashing blue sign” indicating the robot can’t see a label. [Image support needed: visual of the robot/indicator showing flashing blue.]

In the flashing-blue case, perform the source-described physical recovery: E stop the system, walk into the floor, and push the robot onto the label. [Image support needed: photo/figure showing the robot being pushed onto a label location and the relevant E-stop control location/label.]

After the robot identifies the label, observe the documented indicator transition: it should go from flashing blue to solid blue. [Image support needed: indicator transition from flashing blue to solid blue.]
Clear the E stop and verify the robot is successfully showing on the map. [Image support needed: map view where the robot appears successfully after clearing E stop.]

If the robot is in the restart cycle state described as “solid green,” wait until it turns green before moving it because brakes stay locked. [Image support needed: indicator showing solid green and/or the point when it turns green/ready state.]
structured_payload.expected_result: When the robot cannot see a label after restart, the flashing blue indicator changes to solid blue after being pushed onto the label; after clearing E stop, the robot appears successfully on the map.
failure_or_escalation_notes: Escalate if the indicator does not transition from flashing blue to solid blue after pushing the robot onto the label, or if the robot still does not appear on the map after clearing E stop.
Do not attempt to move the robot while brakes are described as locked (e.g., when not in the expected green state).
access_or_tools_needed: Physical floor access to push the robot onto the label
Physical E-stop control (operator only)
RMS / fleet status UI map view and robot indicator visibility

extraction_notes: This is a recovery candidate derived from the segment’s described physical steps and observable indicator color transitions.
The source does not provide exact UI/screen names for the indicator; inline image notes are included to capture the flashing blue/solid blue/solid green evidence.

structured_payload.title: Use Map Robot Selection “Go to” to reposition an AGV to a selected square
structured_payload.candidate_goal: Send an AGV that is not currently in a task to a chosen map square using the Robot Selection “Go to” function, to recover quickly from a stuck/blocked situation.
structured_payload.summary: The source describes a map-based Robot Selection workflow where you select an AGV, choose “Go to,” select a destination square, and confirm. It also notes the use case of recovering quickly when an AGV will not leave an area (example given: a tipper goes down).
rough_steps: Open the OptiSweep map view that supports selecting operational objects (not just clicking on the map background). [Image support needed: screenshot/frame showing the map with selectable objects and the “Robot Selection” UI controls.]
Select the specific AGV object on the map (not a generic map click). [Image support needed: frame showing an AGV selected on the map.]
Select the “Go to” function for the selected AGV. [Image support needed: frame showing the “Go to” option/button after selecting an AGV.]
Select the destination square on the map where you want the AGV to go. [Image support needed: frame showing destination square selection.]

content.text: In the RMS/map view, rack locations use two distinct colors to indicate tote presence. Dark blue/violet indicates a tote is on the rack; light blue indicates the rack is empty. This helps verify whether a tote addition/removal issue is reflected in the system.

structured_payload.title: Identify tote presence at sorter rack locations using RMS rack color (dark blue vs light blue)
structured_payload.candidate_goal: Use the RMS rack location color to determine whether a rack position is expected to have a tote present or is empty, and flag mismatches when a tote should exist at a sorter destination.
structured_payload.summary: In the RMS/map view, rack locations use two distinct colors to indicate tote presence. Dark blue/violet indicates a tote is on the rack; light blue indicates the rack is empty. This helps verify whether a tote addition/removal issue is reflected in the system.
rough_steps: Open the RMS / fleet status UI (RMS/map view) and locate the sorter destination rack locations on the map. [Image support needed: RMS/map view showing rack locations with dark blue/violet vs light blue.]
Visually check the rack location color for the specific rack position you are investigating.
If the rack is dark blue (almost like violet), treat it as “tote present on the rack.”
If the rack is light blue, treat it as “rack empty / no tote on the rack.”
Compare the observed rack color to what you expect to be present at that sorter destination (e.g., you expect a tote there but see light blue).
Stop and escalate if the rack color indicates “empty” (light blue) where a tote should be present, suggesting a tote addition/removal process problem.
structured_payload.expected_result: The rack location color in RMS matches the documented meaning: dark blue/violet = tote present; light blue = rack empty.
failure_or_escalation_notes: Escalate if the rack color does not match the expected tote presence for the destination you are checking (e.g., expected tote but rack shows light blue).
access_or_tools_needed: RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui)

structured_payload.candidate_goal: Verify what exchange type a tote task is performing and whether it is ready for exchange, including key identifiers (Tote ID, AGV ID, Station, Task ID, Task Name) and any tote error state.
structured_payload.summary: Use the AVEVA HMI Tote Tasks view to inspect the current tote task’s exchange-related fields (exchange type, priority, original destination, ready-for-exchange) and confirm the associated tote/task identifiers and any tote error.
rough_steps: Open the AVEVA HMI screen that shows the “Tote Tasks” / “Tote Task” interface. [Image support needed: the AVEVA HMI “Tote Tasks Aveva API page” screen with the Tote Task fields visible.]

Locate and read the tote task identifiers/fields shown on the Tote Task interface: Tote Id, AGV Id, Original Destination, Station, Task id, Task Name, and Tote Error. [Image support needed: the same screen showing these labeled fields/columns.]

Check the exchange-related fields on the same Tote Task interface: exchange type, whether the exchange is marked as priority, and whether it is “ready for exchange.” [Image support needed: the same screen showing exchange type/priority/ready-for-exchange indicators.]

If the interface indicates an AUV behind it is ready to go, confirm which station(s) are listed for that tote task and whether it is associated with the “sorter task UID.” [Image support needed: the same screen showing station(s) and any “sorter task UID” field/value.]

If Tote Error is populated (non-empty / not “no error”), note the error value and the associated Tote Id / Task Name so support can reference the exact tote task. [Image support needed: the Tote Error field showing an error value versus blank/normal state.]
Stop when you have recorded the current Tote Id, Task Name, exchange type, priority flag, ready-for-exchange status, Original Destination, Station, and Tote Error (if present).
structured_payload.expected_result: The AVEVA HMI Tote Task interface displays the current tote task’s exchange type and readiness status (“ready for exchange”), along with the tote/task identifiers (Tote Id, AGV Id, Original Destination, Station, Task id, Task Name) and a Tote Error field that is either empty/normal or contains an error value.
failure_or_escalation_notes: Escalate to FORTNA support if the Tote Error field indicates an error for the tote task you are investigating, or if the exchange readiness status does not align with the expected operational behavior on the floor.

If the Tote Tasks screen does not show the expected fields (Tote Id, AGV Id, Original Destination, Station, Task id, Task Name, Tote Error), stop and escalate because the required live evidence is not visible.

content.text: Use the AVEVA HMI “Initialize Tote” API page to submit an initialization request for a tote and confirm the outcome via the on-screen Response field (confirmation on success; error/tote status on failure).

structured_payload.title: Initialize a Tote Using the Aveva API “Initialize Tote” Page (Request + Response Check)
structured_payload.candidate_goal: Initialize a tote in the system by entering BarcodeID/Code ID, StationID, and ToteID, then verify success or capture the failure reason from the Response field.
structured_payload.summary: Use the AVEVA HMI “Initialize Tote” API page to submit an initialization request for a tote and confirm the outcome via the on-screen Response field (confirmation on success; error/tote status on failure).
rough_steps: Open the AVEVA HMI page labeled “Initialize Tote” (Aveva API page). [Image support needed: screenshot/figure showing the “Initialize Tote Aveva API page” with the input fields and “Request to Initialize Tote” button.]
In the BarcodeID field, enter the tote barcode value (the source states BarcodeID and Code ID use the same number). [Image support needed: the BarcodeID and Code ID fields visible on the page.]

In the StationID field, enter the station ID for the rack station (the source notes StationID corresponds to station IDs shown in RMS). [Image support needed: the StationID field visible with an example/label.]
In the ToteID field, enter the tote ID. [Image support needed: the ToteID field visible with an example/label.]
Click the button labeled “Request to Initialize Tote”. [Image support needed: the “Request to Initialize Tote” button location and label.]

Observe the “Response” field after the request completes: confirm whether it shows a confirmation message (success) or an error message / tote status (failure). [Image support needed: the Response field showing both success confirmation and failure error/tote status states.]

If the response indicates the tote cannot be initialized, check whether the source-provided failure context applies: totes on an AGV may be rejected; also failures can indicate AGVs not in the system or AGVs that have been removed, and the response may include a tote status explaining why initialization failed. [Image support needed: example response text/state for “can’t be initialized” and tote status reason.]
structured_payload.expected_result: After clicking “Request to Initialize Tote,” the “Response” field displays either (1) a confirmation message indicating the tote was initialized successfully, or (2) an error message / tote status explaining why initialization failed (e.g., AGV-related conditions such as AGVs not in the system or removed).
failure_or_escalation_notes: Stop and escalate if the Response field shows an initialization failure and you cannot determine the tote status reason from the displayed error/tote status text.
If the response indicates AGV-related rejection (totes on an AGV), do not proceed with repeated initialization attempts without addressing the AGV condition implied by the response.
access_or_tools_needed: AVEVA HMI (Initialize Tote page / Aveva API page)

source_refs.quote_or_summary: Initialize Tote Aveva API page: enter BarcodeID/Code ID, StationID, ToteID; click “Request to Initialize Tote”; check “Response” field for confirmation or error/tote status; failures may occur when totes are on AGVs, or when AGVs are not in the system or removed.

content.text: Diagnose why a front AGV moved out without a replacement/backfill by checking (1) whether the trailing AGV had a fault (including the case where it was reported ready for a new task and faulted at the same time) and (2) whether chute closure/fullness and exchange timing targets indicate exchanges were not completed before chute closure.

structured_payload.title: Diagnose AGV exchange/backfill gap when an AGV moves out without a replacement
structured_payload.summary: Diagnose why a front AGV moved out without a replacement/backfill by checking (1) whether the trailing AGV had a fault (including the case where it was reported ready for a new task and faulted at the same time) and (2) whether chute closure/fullness and exchange timing targets indicate exchanges were not completed before chute closure.
structured_payload.when_to_use: Use when you observe or are told that an AGV moved out without another AGV backfilling/replacing it during an exchange, and you need live evidence to confirm whether the trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing and/or chute fullness/closure and exchange timing targets contributed.
not_for: Do not use this procedure as a substitute for physical safety actions (e.g., E-stop/LOTO).
roles_and_responsibilities: L2_support: Perform RMS and WCS/Helix DB (SSMS) checks to confirm trailing AGV fault/backfill failure evidence and chute fullness/exchange timing evidence.
access_or_tools_needed: RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui)
WCS / Helix DB (SSMS) (wcs_sql)

system_preconditions: You have an exchange event context to identify the AGV pair (front AGV that moved out and trailing AGV that should have backfilled) and the relevant time window.

visual_references.description: Training frame describing the mechanism: front AGV will not move until trailing AGV is present; software sends both commands together; gap can occur if trailing AGV faults (possibly while also being ready); chute gets closed when full; exchange timing targets (median ~8s, floor ~6.7s).
Training frame describing exchange thresholds and that exchanges are staged with strict quick KPI targets (context for exchange timing/threshold behavior).
Training frame describing system-level API page concepts (context only; not specific to this diagnostic’s live checks).

steps.title: Open RMS / fleet status UI and identify the AGV pair for the exchange event
steps.purpose: Establish which front AGV moved out and which trailing AGV should have backfilled so you can check the trailing AGV’s fault/ready+fault timing.
steps.instruction: Using the RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui), locate the AGV pair involved in the exchange event: the AGV that moved out (front) and the AGV that should have backfilled (trailing).
steps.expected_result: You have identified the specific trailing AGV associated with the exchange event time window (so you can check whether it faulted when the front AGV moved out).
steps.healthy_condition: The RMS view clearly shows the relevant AGVs and their status/error context for the exchange event you are investigating.
steps.failure_condition: You cannot determine which trailing AGV corresponds to the exchange event, or RMS does not provide enough context to identify the correct AGV pair/time window.

actions.label: Locate AGV pair in RMS
actions.exact_action: Open RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui) and locate the AGV pair involved in the exchange event (the AGV that moved out and the AGV that should have backfilled).

stop_or_escalate_if: If you cannot identify the correct AGV pair/time window in RMS, proceed to WCS/Helix DB (SSMS) (wcs_sql) to find the relevant AGV records for the time window.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Front AGV will not move until AGV behind it; software sends both commands at the same time; there has to be one behind it for the software to even send the command to leave.

steps.title: Check trailing AGV status for fault at the time the front AGV moved out
steps.purpose: Confirm the causal mechanism: the only time the front AGV can move without replacement is when the trailing AGV has a fault (including the case where it was ready and faulted at the same time).
steps.instruction: In RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui), check the trailing (behind) AGV’s status/error indicators around the time the front AGV moved out. Confirm whether the trailing AGV is faulted, or shows a fault coincident with being reported ready for a new task.
steps.expected_result: You find live evidence that the trailing AGV had an active fault at (or coincident with) the time the front AGV moved out, consistent with the described pairing/backfill failure mechanism.
steps.healthy_condition: Trailing AGV shows no fault at the relevant time (or fault timing does not coincide with the front AGV move-out), suggesting the gap may be explained by other factors (e.g., chute fullness/exchange timing).
steps.failure_condition: Trailing AGV fault evidence is unclear or absent in RMS for the relevant time window.

actions.label: Verify trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing
actions.exact_action: Check the trailing (behind) AGV status for a fault at the time the front AGV moved out; confirm whether the trailing AGV is faulted (or shows a fault coincident with being “ready for a new task”).

stop_or_escalate_if: If you confirm trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing that would prevent proper backfill, stop further fault/backfill investigation and proceed to escalation guidance.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Only time it can happen is if the AGV behind it has a fault because the front AGV will not move until AGV behind it. Software sends both commands at the same time. Sometimes the AGV behind it is ready for a new task and it might have completed and faulted at the same time.

steps.title: If RMS is inconclusive, query WCS / Helix DB (SSMS) for trailing AGV fault/backfill failure evidence
steps.purpose: Provide database-backed evidence when RMS does not show a clear fault/backfill failure for the trailing AGV at the relevant time.
steps.instruction: Using WCS / Helix DB (SSMS) (wcs_sql), query the OptiSweep DB for the same time window to find evidence of a fault/backfill failure for the trailing AGV (e.g., AGV state/error records).
steps.expected_result: You identify live database evidence that the trailing AGV faulted (or otherwise failed to support backfill) during the exchange window corresponding to the front AGV move-out.
steps.healthy_condition: Database records show no fault/backfill failure for the trailing AGV in the relevant time window, shifting focus to chute fullness/closure and exchange timing.
steps.failure_condition: Database records do not show any trailing AGV fault/backfill failure evidence for the relevant time window.

actions.label: Query trailing AGV state/error records
actions.exact_action: If RMS shows no clear fault, use WCS / Helix DB (SSMS) (wcs_sql) to query the relevant OptiSweep DB tables/models for the same time window to find evidence of a fault/backfill failure for the trailing AGV (e.g., AGV state/error records).

stop_or_escalate_if: If you confirm trailing AGV fault/backfill failure evidence in the database, stop further chute/timing checks and proceed to escalation guidance.
If you do not find trailing AGV fault/backfill failure evidence, proceed to chute fullness/exchange timing checks.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Only time it can happen is if the AGV behind it has a fault... so sometimes it... completed and faulted at the same time. (Mechanism to corroborate with live data.)

steps.title: Check chute fullness/closure and exchange timing targets around the event
steps.purpose: Validate the alternative contributing mechanism: chute closure is fullness-driven, and exchanges should complete before reaching 80% (median ~8s, floor ~6.7s).
steps.instruction: Using WCS / Helix DB (SSMS) (wcs_sql), review live system data available for chute fullness and exchange timing metrics around the event time window. Look for conditions consistent with chute closure when the chute is full and exchange not completing before the 80% threshold (with exchange timing deviating from the median ~8 seconds and floor ~6.7 seconds).
steps.expected_result: You find live evidence that chute fullness/closure occurred (or was imminent) such that exchanges were not completed before the 80% threshold, and/or exchange timing deviated from the described targets (median ~8s, floor ~6.7s).
steps.healthy_condition: Chute fullness/closure did not occur before exchanges completed, and exchange timing aligns with the described targets (median ~8s, floor ~6.7s).
steps.failure_condition: Chute fullness/closure and exchange timing metrics do not align with the described mechanisms (i.e., no evidence of fullness-driven closure or timing deviation).

actions.label: Review chute fullness and exchange timing metrics
actions.exact_action: Check whether chute closure/fullness conditions could have occurred by reviewing live system data available via WCS/Helix DB (wcs_sql) for chute fullness / exchange timing metrics around the event; look for conditions consistent with “chute gets closed when the chute is full” and exchange not completing before the 80% threshold.

stop_or_escalate_if: If you confirm chute fullness/insufficient exchange rate consistent with chute closure before exchange completion, stop and escalate.
If chute fullness/exchange timing metrics do not align with the described mechanisms, escalate because the cause is not confirmed by the available evidence.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Chute gets closed when the chute is full... thresholds we stage for an exchange and before we hit that 80%, we've already done the exchange... goal is a median 8 second exchange time... floor is like 6.7 seconds... trying to do it before we close the chute.

steps.title: Stop and escalate based on confirmed evidence (or lack of evidence)
steps.purpose: Ensure the diagnostic outcome is actionable: either confirm the described mechanism with evidence or escalate when evidence is missing.
steps.instruction: Based on your findings from RMS and WCS/Helix DB, decide whether to escalate. Escalate when you confirm the trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing mechanism or confirm chute fullness/insufficient exchange timing mechanism, or when you cannot confirm either mechanism with live evidence.
steps.expected_result: A clear diagnostic conclusion is produced: (1) trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing explains the missing backfill, and/or (2) chute fullness/closure and exchange timing targets indicate exchanges were not completed before 80%. If neither is supported by live evidence, escalation occurs due to unconfirmed cause.
steps.healthy_condition: Evidence supports one or both mechanisms described (trailing AGV fault timing and/or fullness-driven chute closure with exchange timing deviation).
steps.failure_condition: No live evidence supports trailing AGV fault/backfill failure and no live evidence supports chute fullness/closure or exchange timing deviation.

actions.label: Escalate with evidence
actions.exact_action: Stop and escalate if you confirm the trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing that would prevent proper backfill, or if you confirm chute fullness/insufficient tipping/exchange rate consistent with chute closure before exchange completion.

stop_or_escalate_if: Escalate if RMS and WCS/Helix DB do not show a trailing AGV fault/backfill failure and chute fullness/exchange timing metrics do not align with the described mechanisms.
Do not assume the cause solely from the event description; require live fault/state evidence for the trailing AGV and/or live chute fullness/exchange timing evidence.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: Mechanism statements: trailing AGV fault prevents proper backfill; chute closes when full; exchange staged before 80% with median ~8s and floor ~6.7s.

success_criteria: You confirm (with live RMS and/or WCS/Helix DB evidence) that the trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing explains why the front AGV moved out without replacement/backfill.

OR you confirm (with live WCS/Helix DB evidence) that chute fullness/closure occurred such that exchanges were not completed before the 80% threshold, with exchange timing deviating from the described targets (median ~8s, floor ~6.7s).
If neither mechanism is supported by live evidence, you escalate rather than assuming the cause.
healthy_conditions: Trailing AGV does not show a fault coincident with the front AGV move-out, and/or database records do not show trailing AGV fault/backfill failure in the relevant time window.
Chute fullness/closure does not occur before exchanges complete; exchange timing aligns with median ~8s and floor ~6.7s targets.
failure_conditions: Trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing is present at the time the front AGV moved out, consistent with missing backfill.
Chute fullness/closure occurs (or is imminent) such that exchanges were not completed before reaching 80%, with exchange timing deviating from median ~8s and floor ~6.7s.
RMS and WCS/Helix DB show no trailing AGV fault/backfill failure evidence and no chute fullness/exchange timing evidence consistent with the described mechanisms.
escalation_guidance: Escalate if you confirm the trailing AGV fault/ready+fault timing mechanism or confirm chute fullness/insufficient exchange timing consistent with chute closure before exchange completion.

Escalate if RMS and WCS/Helix DB do not show trailing AGV fault/backfill failure and chute fullness/exchange timing metrics do not align with the described mechanisms (do not assume the cause from the event description alone).

source_refs.quote_or_summary: Has this ever happened that an AGV moves out without another one to replace it?... only time it can happen is if the AGV behind it has a fault... software sends both commands at the same time... chute gets closed when the chute is full... thresholds stage for an exchange and before we hit that 80%, we've already done the exchange... goal median 8 second exchange time... floor 6.7 seconds.

content.text: Use the RMS / fleet status UI to determine whether AGVs are not progressing due to state-transition failure visibility patterns: (1) AGVs waiting to do an exchange during shutdown, and/or (2) startup delay while waiting for an AGV on the charger. The system is described as exposing this via system faults and visible waiting conditions.

structured_payload.title: Check RMS / fleet status UI for AGVs waiting to exchange during shutdown or startup delay waiting on charger
structured_payload.summary: Use the RMS / fleet status UI to determine whether AGVs are not progressing due to state-transition failure visibility patterns: (1) AGVs waiting to do an exchange during shutdown, and/or (2) startup delay while waiting for an AGV on the charger. The system is described as exposing this via system faults and visible waiting conditions.
structured_payload.when_to_use: Use when lifecycle progression appears delayed during shutdown/startup and you need to check whether RMS is showing AGVs in the documented waiting/fault visibility patterns (exchange-waiting during shutdown; charger-waiting startup delay).
roles_and_responsibilities: L1_support: Execute the RMS / fleet status UI checks for waiting conditions and any visible system faults/alerts that align with the described state-transition failure patterns.
access_or_tools_needed: RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui)

system_preconditions: RMS / fleet status UI is reachable and displaying fleet/AGV status and any faults/alerts.

visual_references.description: Training segment frame used as evidence that the system will show faults/visible waiting conditions for (a) AGV waiting to do an exchange during shutdown and (b) startup delay waiting for an AGV on the charger.

steps.title: Open RMS / fleet status UI and navigate to AGV status/errors overview
steps.purpose: Get to the live area where AGV waiting conditions and system faults/alerts are visible for diagnosis.
steps.instruction: Open the RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui) and navigate to the AGV status/errors overview area.
steps.expected_result: You are viewing the RMS AGV status/errors overview area where AGV waiting conditions and system fault/alert visibility can be checked.
steps.healthy_condition: The RMS AGV status/errors overview area is populated and ready for inspection (not blank/unreachable).
steps.failure_condition: RMS is unreachable, the AGV status/errors overview area is blank, or you cannot view any fault/alert visibility needed for the diagnosis.

actions.label: Open RMS fleet status UI
actions.exact_action: Open the RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui) and navigate to the AGV status/errors overview area.

stop_or_escalate_if: RMS / fleet status UI cannot be accessed or the AGV status/errors overview area is not viewable.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “System faults are visible; examples include an AGV waiting to do an exchange during shutdown and startup delay waiting for an AGV on the charger.”

steps.title: Check for AGVs waiting to do an exchange during shutdown
steps.purpose: Identify the shutdown-related waiting condition described as visible in system faults/AGV waiting states.
steps.instruction: In the RMS AGV status/errors overview, look for AGVs showing a waiting condition consistent with “waiting to do an exchange” during shutdown.
steps.expected_result: At least one AGV is indicated in RMS as waiting to do an exchange during shutdown (or you determine none are indicated).
steps.healthy_condition: No widespread exchange-waiting indications are present when shutdown is expected to complete normally.
steps.failure_condition: You see one or more AGVs indicated as waiting to do an exchange during shutdown, especially if repeated/widespread.

actions.label: Inspect exchange-waiting indications
actions.exact_action: Look for AGVs showing a waiting condition consistent with “waiting to do an exchange” during shutdown.

stop_or_escalate_if: You observe repeated or widespread exchange-waiting indications that prevent lifecycle progression.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “if you try to shut down, you can see, … an AGVS waiting to do an exchange”

steps.title: Check for startup delay waiting for an AGV on the charger
steps.purpose: Identify the startup-related waiting condition described as visible in system faults/AGV waiting states.
steps.instruction: In the RMS AGV status/errors overview, look for startup delay evidence consistent with “waiting … for an AGV on the charger.”
steps.expected_result: At least one AGV is indicated in RMS as contributing to startup delay by waiting for an AGV on the charger (or you determine none are indicated).
steps.healthy_condition: No charger-waiting startup delay indications are present when startup proceeds normally.
steps.failure_condition: You see indications consistent with startup delay while waiting for an AGV on the charger, especially if repeated/widespread.

actions.label: Inspect charger-waiting indications
actions.exact_action: Look for startup delay evidence consistent with “waiting … for an AGV on the charger.”

stop_or_escalate_if: You observe repeated or widespread charger-waiting indications that prevent lifecycle progression.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “when you start up, … delay because it’s waiting … from an AGV on the charger”

steps.title: Confirm system faults/alerts align with the waiting conditions
steps.purpose: Validate that RMS is reporting faults/alerts that correspond to the described waiting/failure visibility patterns.
steps.instruction: In the RMS AGV status/errors overview, confirm whether system faults/alerts are visible and align with the exchange-waiting and/or charger-waiting conditions you observed.
steps.expected_result: RMS shows visible system fault/alert entries that align with the waiting conditions (or you determine there are no aligning fault/alert entries).
steps.healthy_condition: Fault/alert visibility is consistent with normal operation (no fault entries that match the described waiting patterns).
steps.failure_condition: Fault/alert visibility is present and aligns with exchange-waiting and/or charger-waiting indications, especially if repeated/widespread.

actions.label: Inspect fault/alert visibility
actions.exact_action: Confirm whether the system is reporting faults/alerts that align with the above waiting conditions (system faults are explicitly mentioned as visible).

stop_or_escalate_if: You see repeated or widespread waiting/fault indications that prevent lifecycle progression.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “the system faults… System faults are visible… an AGVS waiting to do an exchange… startup… delay… waiting… from an AGV on the charger”

steps.title: Stop and escalate on repeated or widespread waiting/fault indications
steps.purpose: Avoid spending time on further surface-level checks when the described failure visibility patterns are clearly preventing lifecycle progression.
steps.instruction: If you see repeated or widespread waiting/fault indications that prevent lifecycle progression (e.g., multiple AGVs stuck in exchange-waiting or charger-waiting states), stop and escalate for deeper investigation.
steps.expected_result: Escalation is initiated when the RMS evidence shows repeated/widespread waiting/fault indications consistent with the described patterns.
steps.healthy_condition: No repeated/widespread waiting/fault indications are present; lifecycle progression is not blocked by the described patterns.
steps.failure_condition: Repeated/widespread waiting/fault indications are present and escalation is not initiated.

actions.label: Escalate
actions.exact_action: Stop and escalate if you see repeated or widespread waiting/fault indications that prevent lifecycle progression (e.g., multiple AGVs stuck in exchange-waiting or charger-waiting states).

stop_or_escalate_if: Multiple AGVs stuck in exchange-waiting during shutdown.
Multiple AGVs stuck in charger-waiting during startup delay.
System faults/alerts visible in RMS align with these waiting conditions and are repeated/widespread.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “the system will tell you… an AGVS waiting to do an exchange… delay… waiting… from an AGV on the charger”

success_criteria: RMS / fleet status UI shows either (a) AGVs indicated as waiting to do an exchange during shutdown and/or (b) startup delay evidence consistent with waiting for an AGV on the charger.
RMS also shows visible system faults/alerts that align with the observed waiting conditions (when present).
healthy_conditions: RMS does not show widespread exchange-waiting indications during shutdown.
RMS does not show charger-waiting startup delay indications.
RMS fault/alert visibility does not align with the described waiting patterns.
failure_conditions: RMS shows repeated/widespread AGVs waiting to do an exchange during shutdown.
RMS shows repeated/widespread startup delay evidence consistent with waiting for an AGV on the charger.
RMS shows system faults/alerts that align with the above waiting conditions.
escalation_guidance: If RMS does not show any fault/waiting evidence while lifecycle progression is failing, escalate for deeper investigation (the segment only states the system will tell you via faults/waiting conditions, but does not provide additional surfaces here).

screens_or_images.description: Training frame evidence for the two waiting/fault visibility patterns: exchange-waiting during shutdown and charger-waiting startup delay.

source_refs.quote_or_summary: “System faults are visible; examples include an AGV waiting to do an exchange during shutdown and startup delay waiting for an AGV on the charger.”

content.text: Use the Geek+ RMS / fleet status web UI to confirm the overall page is reachable and that it correctly separates fault categories: “system faults” on the left and “AGV system faults” on the right. If the RMS page is blank, treat it as a reachability/firewall symptom. Use the left/right placement to interpret whether the issue is communication loss vs an AGV that was commanded to move but is not in progress.

steps.title: Interpret left/right fault placement for communication loss vs commanded-but-not-in-progress movement
steps.purpose: Use the fault placement to understand the likely category of the underlying issue.
steps.instruction: Use the source mapping: if you lose communication with a chat, expect it on the left “system faults”; if you told an AGV to move but it hasn’t moved, expect it on the right “AGV system faults”.
steps.expected_result: You can map the observed fault placement to either communication-loss (left) or commanded-but-not-in-progress movement (right).
steps.healthy_condition: Observed faults align with the expected left/right meaning (left = communication loss; right = commanded move not in progress).
steps.failure_condition: Fault placement does not align with the expected left/right meaning described by the source.

actions.label: Map fault placement to meaning
actions.exact_action: Use the source mapping to interpret placement: if communication loss with a chat occurs, expect it on the left “system faults”; if an AGV was told to move but it has not moved/in progress, expect it on the right “AGV system faults”.

stop_or_escalate_if: Fault placement does not match the expected left/right meaning described by the source.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: If we lose communication with one of the chats, it'll be on the left. If we told an AGV to move but it hasn't moved, it'll be on the right.

healthy_conditions: RMS overall page shows the expected two fault areas: system faults on the left and active AGV system faults on the right.
If the RMS page is blank, it matches the firewall-not-open symptom described by the source.
failure_conditions: RMS remains blank (no visible system/AGV fault panels).
Left/right fault separation is not observable or does not align with the expected meaning (left = communication loss; right = commanded move not in progress).
escalation_guidance: If RMS remains blank (no visible system/AGV fault panels), escalate as a firewall/reachability issue consistent with the source symptom.
If the left/right fault placement does not match the expected meaning described by the source, escalate for further investigation of RMS fault categorization/communication behavior.

content.text: Use RMS Charger Selection to logically disable a specific charging location (by charger ID) so RMS will not route AGVs to it. Physically place a low-power AGV onto that disabled charger for a charging boost, then re-enable the charger so RMS/WCS can resume charging allocation from the charging queue.

structured_payload.title: Disable/Enable a Charging Location From RMS Charger Selection to Manually Charge a Low-Power AGV
structured_payload.summary: Use RMS Charger Selection to logically disable a specific charging location (by charger ID) so RMS will not route AGVs to it. Physically place a low-power AGV onto that disabled charger for a charging boost, then re-enable the charger so RMS/WCS can resume charging allocation from the charging queue.
structured_payload.when_to_use: When an AGV’s power is extremely low (e.g., stuck in an error state too long) and you need to manually place it onto a charger for a charging boost by preventing RMS from routing other AGVs to that charger.
roles_and_responsibilities: L2_support: Execute the RMS Charger Selection disable/enable actions and verify the charger status changes as expected.
safety_notes: Disabling a charger is a logical allocation control (it does not “kill” the charger hardware).
access_or_tools_needed: RMS / fleet status UI (rms_ui) with Charger Selection view

system_preconditions: The target charging station has a unique charger ID visible in RMS Charger Selection.

visual_references.description: RMS Charger Selection frame showing charger selection by charger ID and the concept of enabled/disabled charger status for logical allocation control.

content.text: On the RMS / fleet status UI map monitor summary, read the “count of AGVs disconnected” metric. structured_payload.title: Check RMS disconnected AGV count and identify likely disconnect cause (lost RMS comms vs turned off)
structured_payload.summary: On the RMS / fleet status UI map monitor summary, read the “count of AGVs disconnected” metric. Use the training’s definition to interpret “disconnected” as AGVs that have lost communication from RMS (RMS runs on the server; AGVs are on Wi‑Fi), then correlate the disconnected count with likely causes: Wi‑Fi/RMS communication loss vs AGVs being turned off.
structured_payload.when_to_use: When you need a first-pass diagnostic using RMS’s disconnected AGV count to understand whether AGVs are likely disconnected due to lost RMS/Wi‑Fi communication versus being turned off.
not_for: Do not use this procedure as the only evidence to confirm a specific root cause when the disconnected count is high and you cannot determine whether it is communication loss or AGVs being turned off (requires additional evidence beyond this metric).
roles_and_responsibilities: L1_support: Execute the RMS / fleet status UI checks and interpret the disconnected AGV count using the provided definition.
L2_support: Assist when the disconnected count is high and the cause cannot be determined from this metric alone.

content.text: Use the RMS/map view rack location color to determine whether a sorter rack position is expected to have a tote present or is empty. Use this to flag mismatches when a tote should exist at a sorter destination but the map shows the empty color.
structured_payload.when_to_use: When investigating a suspected tote addition/removal mismatch at a sorter destination and you need a quick, visual confirmation of tote presence/absence at specific rack locations in the RMS/map view.

steps.title: Interpret rack color as tote present vs empty
steps.purpose: Convert the RMS rack color into an observable tote presence/absence state.
steps.instruction: Visually check the rack location color for the specific rack position you are investigating and interpret it using the RMS color meaning: dark blue/violet = tote present; light blue = rack empty.
steps.expected_result: For the rack position you are investigating, you determine one of two states based on color: dark blue/violet (tote present) or light blue (rack empty).
steps.healthy_condition: The rack color interpretation is unambiguous: dark blue/violet corresponds to tote present; light blue corresponds to empty.
steps.failure_condition: The rack color does not clearly match either tone (ambiguous/unclear display), or the color interpretation cannot be made reliably for the rack position.

actions.label: Check for dark blue/violet vs light blue

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: If a rack has this dark blue tone, it means it has a toad on it. If it has the light blue tone, it means it's empty.

steps.title: Compare observed rack color to expected tote presence at the destination
steps.purpose: Determine whether the RMS map reflects the expected tote addition/removal state for the sorter destination.
steps.instruction: Compare the observed rack color state (tote present vs empty) to what you expect to be present at that sorter destination (for example, you expect a tote there but the rack shows light blue).
steps.expected_result: You conclude whether the rack color matches expected tote presence or indicates a mismatch (expected tote but observed empty/light blue).
steps.healthy_condition: Observed rack color matches expectation (dark blue/violet when a tote is expected; light blue when no tote is expected).
steps.failure_condition: Observed rack color indicates empty (light blue) where a tote is expected, suggesting a tote addition/removal process problem.

actions.label: Validate against expectation

content.text: If a robot is restarted but does not snap back onto the map because it cannot see a label, use the documented indicator color behavior (flashing blue → solid blue; solid green indicates restart cycle/brakes locked) and perform the source-described physical label reacquisition steps. Then clear the E stop and confirm the robot appears successfully on the map.

structured_payload.title: Handle restart when robot cannot see a label: use indicator color states and verify map visibility after label reacquisition
structured_payload.summary: If a robot is restarted but does not snap back onto the map because it cannot see a label, use the documented indicator color behavior (flashing blue → solid blue; solid green indicates restart cycle/brakes locked) and perform the source-described physical label reacquisition steps. Then clear the E stop and confirm the robot appears successfully on the map.
structured_payload.when_to_use: Use when a robot was restarted but does not automatically snap back onto the map because it cannot see a label.
roles_and_responsibilities: Operator: Perform physical E-stop actions and physical label reacquisition (push robot onto the label) and then clear E stop to verify map recovery.
safety_notes: Operator-only physical E-stop actions are required for the flashing-blue label reacquisition path.
access_or_tools_needed: Physical floor access to push the robot onto the label
Physical E-stop control (operator only)
RMS / fleet status UI map view and robot indicator visibility

system_preconditions: Robot has been restarted and is not snapping back onto the map automatically

visual_references.description: Restart recovery segment showing the restart flow, the flashing blue sign (cannot see a label), the flashing blue → solid blue transition, and the solid green/brakes locked behavior.

steps.title: Check whether the restarted robot snaps back onto the map
steps.purpose: Determine whether the robot recovered automatically after restart or needs label reacquisition.
steps.instruction: On the RMS / fleet status UI map view, observe whether the restarted robot is displayed/positioned on the map.
steps.expected_result: The robot is either displayed on the map (automatic recovery) or not displayed/positioned (needs further recovery steps).
steps.healthy_condition: After restart, the robot appears on the map.
steps.failure_condition: The robot does not snap back onto the map automatically after restart.

actions.label: Inspect map visibility for restarted robot
actions.exact_action: Check whether the robot snaps back onto the map automatically.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “If your robot is stopped for some reason in between two labels and you perform a restart, it will not snap back onto the map automatically.”

steps.title: If robot is not on the map, identify the flashing blue indicator state (cannot see a label)
steps.purpose: Confirm the documented cause for missing map visibility: the robot cannot see a label.
steps.instruction: Locate the robot’s indicator and look for the documented “flashing blue sign” state indicating the robot can’t see a label.
steps.expected_result: You observe the flashing blue indicator state when the robot cannot see a label.
steps.healthy_condition: Flashing blue corresponds to the robot searching/can’t see a label (as described).
steps.failure_condition: Indicator state does not match the expected flashing blue when the robot is missing from the map (requires escalation/SME guidance).

actions.label: Inspect robot indicator for flashing blue
actions.exact_action: Look for the documented indicator state described as a “flashing blue sign” indicating the robot can’t see a label.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “It's because it can't see a label and you'll see that flashing blue sign.”
Transcript: “...flashing blue sign... E stop the system, walk into the floor, push the robot onto the label...”

steps.title: Perform physical label reacquisition: E stop the system and push the robot onto the label
steps.purpose: Force the robot to identify the label so it can lock on and recover map visibility.
steps.instruction: When the robot is in the flashing blue state, perform the physical recovery: E stop the system, walk into the floor, and push the robot onto the label.
steps.expected_result: After pushing the robot onto the label, the robot identifies the label and its indicator transitions from flashing blue to solid blue.
steps.healthy_condition: Robot is pushed onto the label location and begins label identification.
steps.failure_condition: Robot does not transition from flashing blue to solid blue after being pushed onto the label.

actions.label: E stop the system (operator only)
actions.exact_action: E stop the system.

actions.label: Push robot onto the label
actions.exact_action: walk into the floor, push the robot onto the label.

stop_or_escalate_if: If the indicator does not transition from flashing blue to solid blue after pushing the robot onto the label, escalate.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “In that case, you're, you will have to E stop the system, walk into the floor, push the robot onto the label.”

steps.title: Verify indicator transition from flashing blue to solid blue after label pickup
steps.purpose: Confirm the robot has identified the label and is ready for E-stop clearing and map recovery.
steps.instruction: Observe the robot indicator and confirm it transitions from flashing blue to solid blue after it identifies the label.
steps.expected_result: Indicator goes from flashing blue to solid blue.
steps.healthy_condition: Flashing blue → solid blue transition occurs after label reacquisition.
steps.failure_condition: Indicator remains flashing blue or transitions to an unexpected state instead of solid blue.

actions.label: Inspect indicator color transition
actions.exact_action: observe the documented indicator transition: it should go from flashing blue to solid blue.

stop_or_escalate_if: If the indicator does not transition from flashing blue to solid blue after pushing the robot onto the label, escalate.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “It will go from flashing blue to solid blue because it has picked up...”
Transcript: “...indicator goes flashing blue → solid blue...”

steps.title: Clear E stop and verify the robot is successfully showing on the map
steps.purpose: Complete recovery by clearing E stop and confirming map visibility.
steps.instruction: Clear the E stop, then check the RMS / fleet status UI map view to confirm the robot is successfully showing on the map.
steps.expected_result: After clearing E stop, the robot appears successfully on the map.
steps.healthy_condition: Robot is displayed/positioned on the map after E-stop clear.
steps.failure_condition: Robot still does not appear on the map after clearing E stop.

actions.label: Clear E stop
actions.exact_action: clear the E stop.

actions.label: Verify robot on map
actions.exact_action: you'll see the robot being successfully showing successful on the map itself.

stop_or_escalate_if: If the robot still does not appear on the map after clearing E stop, escalate.

source_evidence.quote_or_summary: “...clear the E stop and you'll see the robot being successfully showing successful on the map itself.”

steps.title: If indicator is solid green, wait until it turns green before moving (brakes stay locked)
steps.purpose: Prevent unsafe movement while the robot’s brakes are described as locked during the restart cycle.
steps.instruction: If the robot is in the restart cycle state described as “solid green,” wait until it turns green before moving it because the brakes stay locked.
